units.title: Step time, token throughput and MFU versus HFU
outcomes: Define step time, tokens per second, MFU and HFU, stating the FLOP count and peak each ratio uses.
Derive tokens per second from step time and batch tokens, and MFU from model FLOPs over peak throughput.
Measure step time and tokens per second with warmup and synchronization, and label CPU timings as non-evidence for GPU interconnects.
units.why: Throughput numbers mean nothing without fixed workload semantics and stated FLOP counts. This unit fixes the definitions before any diagnosis.

next.note: Label the compute, memory or communication bound behind the throughput.
Extend single-rank throughput to scaling efficiency and failure-adjusted goodput.

study.title: MFU versus HFU and FLOP counting
study.locator: MFU vs HFU section with \(\text{HFU} = \text{actual FLOPs} / \text{peak}\) and the `FlopCounterMode` snippet; MFU is a very rough approximation subsection

study.title: Rooflines and the H100 crossover
study.locator: Where Does the Time Go through A Few Problems to Work, with Q1 on intensity and Q5 on the H100 SXM crossover near 295, with answers
study.depth: Keep TPU ICI numbers labeled as TPU numbers. Re-parameterize the crossover for your hardware before quoting it.

study.title: Roofline diagnosis and the MFU definition
study.locator: The Memory Wall and Roofline Diagnosis with the iron law and ridge table, and Measurement at Scale with the MFU bands (40 to 60 percent good, above 60 excellent)

focus: Step time is wall-clock per optimizer step at fixed global batch, sequence length and precision. Tokens per second is global-batch tokens divided by step time.
MFU uses model FLOPs, commonly \(6 N D\) for training, over peak. HFU uses actual FLOPs including recomputation and padding. State both before comparing.
MFU is rough under mixed precision because regions run in different formats while the peak assumes one. Compare before and after on the same setup, never across clusters.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive tokens per second and MFU for \(N = 10^9\) parameters, \(D = 10^6\) tokens and \(T_{step} = 30\) s at peak \(989\) TFLOP/s: tokens/s is about 33,333, model FLOPs are \(6 \times 10^{15}\), achieved about 200 TFLOP/s, MFU about 20 percent.
traps: Comparing MFUs built from different FLOP counts (with versus without attention terms, forward-only versus training) or different peaks (sparse versus dense, BF16 versus FP16).
Reading CPU `gloo` step times as evidence about GPU throughput or interconnects. They check semantics only.
Treating `FlopCounterMode` as exact. It has performance and memory problems and serves as a cross-check, not the answer.

selfTest.q: How are step time, global-batch tokens and tokens per second related?
selfTest.a: Tokens per second is \(D_{tokens} / T_{step}\) at fixed batch, sequence and precision. Change any of the three and the ratio is incomparable.

selfTest.q: Why can HFU exceed MFU on the same run?
selfTest.a: HFU counts actual FLOPs including recomputation, padding and synchronization overhead. MFU counts model FLOPs only, so extra work raises HFU but not MFU.

selfTest.q: A paper reports 55.2 percent MFU on 12,288 GPUs. Can you compare your single-GPU MFU to it?
selfTest.a: No. Different hardware, FLOP-count convention and workload. The 55.2 percent figure is MegaScale's own cluster result for a 175B model, not a transferable target.

selfTest.q: Manual arithmetic and `FlopCounterMode` disagree. Which do you trust?
selfTest.a: The manual count with stated assumptions. The counter is a cross-check with known performance and memory issues.

units.title: Strong and weak scaling efficiency and goodput under failures
outcomes: Define strong scaling, weak scaling and parallel efficiency, stating the fixed quantity in each.
Derive goodput with failures, retries and unusable work for one job size from failure rate and restart cost.
Explain why high device utilization can coexist with poor useful throughput.
units.why: More ranks can raise utilization while lowering useful output once failures, restarts and stragglers dominate. This unit separates busy hardware from finished work.

next.note: Convert goodput into cost per useful token.
Turn failure math into health checks, canaries and runbooks.

study.title: MegaScale scaling and straggler evidence
study.locator: arXiv:2402.15627v1, Sections 4 to 6: heartbeat fault loop, straggler mitigation and 55.2 percent MFU on 12,288 GPUs for a 175B model
study.depth: Treat the MFU and speedup as that cluster's results. Reproduce the method, not the numbers.

study.title: Failure taxonomy and MTTF versus job size
study.locator: arXiv:2410.21680v2, Sections 2 and 5: RSC cluster design, failure taxonomy and MTTF analysis with scheduler-side requeue metrics
study.depth: Model goodput for one job size only. Do not merge these research-cluster numbers with Llama 3 production counts.

focus: Strong scaling fixes the global problem and grows ranks. Weak scaling grows the problem with ranks, usually tokens per GPU. Efficiency is speedup over ranks, or throughput over ranks versus the baseline.
Goodput discounts failed, repeated and unusable work: restarts, preemption, straggler idle and checkpoint overhead. Busy GPUs doing repeated work raise utilization but not goodput.
Failure rate grows with job size, so large jobs pay more checkpoint and restart tax. Every MTTF number is cluster-specific.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute strong-scaling efficiency for \(T_1 = 100\) ms and \(T_4 = 30\) ms: speedup \(100/30 \approx 3.33\), efficiency \(3.33/4 \approx 83\) percent. Then state goodput at 90 percent effective time as \(0.9\) times raw throughput.
traps: Quoting weak-scaling efficiency without stating what is held fixed per rank (tokens, batch or model shard).
Merging interruption counts across studies. Llama 3 Table 5 and the Meta reliability MTTF come from different clusters and mixes.
Treating device utilization as useful throughput when restarts, retries and straggler idle consume the hours.

selfTest.q: What is fixed in strong scaling versus weak scaling?
selfTest.a: Strong scaling fixes the global problem size. Weak scaling grows it with ranks, typically holding tokens or work per rank fixed.

selfTest.q: Four ranks cut step time from 100 ms to 30 ms. What are speedup and efficiency?
selfTest.a: Speedup \(100/30 \approx 3.33\). Efficiency \(3.33/4 \approx 83\) percent against the single-rank baseline.

selfTest.q: How can utilization read 90 percent while goodput is poor?
selfTest.a: GPUs stay busy on repeated, failed or unusable work: restarts after interruptions, straggler waiting, and checkpoint overhead all count as utilized but not useful.

selfTest.q: Why does MTTF fall as job size grows, and what follows for checkpointing?
selfTest.a: More components mean more chances per hour that one fails. Larger jobs need cheaper checkpoints and faster restart because interruptions arrive sooner.

study.title: Continuous benchmarking and logging
study.locator: Chapter 13, Continuous Integration and Performance Benchmarking, with the HUD performance dashboard and MLPerf logging sections

focus: A fixed workload names model, data, global batch, sequence, precision and a correctness check. The Ultra-Scale heatmaps compare configs at one fixed 1M-token workload, never across workloads.
Warmup settles compilation, allocator and cache state. `torch.cuda.synchronize` and a cross-rank barrier separate launch from work. Report raw samples with median and spread from repeated trials.
A manifest records workload hash, config, code version, hardware, backend, environment flags and raw samples. The correctness guard runs with every timing so a fast wrong result fails.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write a benchmark harness for a tiny MLP step that warms up, synchronizes with `torch.cuda.synchronize`, times repeated trials, reports median and spread, and checks the result against a single-process reference within tolerance.
traps: Timing CUDA work without synchronization. Asynchronous launch returns early and measures queueing, not execution.
Reporting one trial or a mean without warmup. Compilation, allocator growth and cache state dominate the first steps.
Changing batch, precision or data between runs and calling the delta a speedup. Fix the workload first.

selfTest.q: Why must the workload stay fixed across a comparison?
selfTest.a: Step time, tokens/s and MFU all depend on model, batch, sequence and precision. Changing any of them changes the work, so the comparison measures a different job.

selfTest.q: What goes wrong when CUDA timing omits synchronization?
selfTest.a: Kernel launches are asynchronous, so the timer stops at enqueue time. The measured time is launch overhead, far below execution time.

selfTest.q: What does warmup settle, and what happens without it?
selfTest.a: Compilation, allocator blocks and cache state. Without warmup the first trials are slower and more variable, and the mean misleads.

selfTest.q: What belongs in a regression evidence manifest?
selfTest.a: Workload identity and hash, configuration, code version, hardware and topology, backend, environment flags, raw timing samples, and the correctness-guard result.

study.title: Systematic profiling and fleet traces
study.locator: System Profiling with the drill from application to operation, and Measurement at Scale on fleet traces and gray stragglers

focus: Split the step into input wait, host transfer, forward and backward kernels, bucket collectives, optimizer and checkpoint. `torch.cuda.nvtx.range_push` and `range_pop` name regions so kernels map to source.
Ranks have skewed clocks, so align by collective entry and exit markers and sequence numbers, never by raw wall-clock order.
The profiler perturbs the run: it can disable fusion and inflate traffic. Compare with and without profiling and state the overhead beside every trace claim.
units.reproduce: Without notes, capture a three-step CPU trace with `torch.profiler.profile`, `record_shapes=True` and NVTX ranges around forward and backward, export the chrome trace, and name the top operation class by time.
traps: Ordering cross-rank events by unsynchronized wall-clock. Clock skew exceeds collective latency, so apparent order is not causal order.
Quoting profiler-inflated memory traffic as hardware truth. Fusion disabled under observation raises HBM passes the real run avoids.
Blaming the network for an NCCL wait when the peer is stalled in the data loader. The waiter is the victim; the straggler is the cause.

selfTest.q: What do NVTX ranges add to a profiler trace?
selfTest.a: Named source regions around forward, backward and transfers. Kernels inside a range inherit its label, so time maps to code instead of anonymous kernels.

selfTest.q: How do you align two rank timelines?
selfTest.a: By shared collective markers with matching sequence numbers and entry or exit events. Raw timestamps cannot order across skewed clocks.

selfTest.q: How do you check profiler overhead?
selfTest.a: Compare step time and key counters with and without the profiler on the same fixed workload. Report the delta beside trace-derived numbers.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 waits in `all_reduce` while rank 1 loads data. Which is the cause?
selfTest.a: Rank 1 input stall is the cause. Rank 0 wait is the victim symptom; fixing the network would not move the step.

study.locator: Enabling Flight Recorder through Analyzing Flight Recorder Dumps, with `TORCH_NCCL_TRACE_BUFFER_SIZE`, `TORCH_NCCL_DUMP_ON_TIMEOUT` and `TORCH_FR_DUMP_TEMP_FILE` (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Hangs with TorchComms and the debug server
study.locator: The Scenario through Running the FR CLI on Per-Rank Pickle Dumps, with `TEST_BACKEND=gloo` and `TEST_DEVICE=cpu` (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: The CPU gloo path is stated but unverified here because `torchcomms` is not installed. Treat dump reading as the exercised skill, not dump collection on CPU.

study.title: Desync reports, recorder traces and NCCL transport logs
study.locator: Diagnosing crashes hangs and tracing execution: The desync report with `TORCH_NCCL_DESYNC_DEBUG`, The flight recorder trace with `TORCH_FR_BUFFER_SIZE` and `TORCH_FR_DUMP_TEMP_FILE`, and `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` with `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS`

focus: The desync report names the rank and collective that fell out of step at timeout. The recorder adds per-rank collective history with Python stacks. Enable both before launching; dumps are post-mortem.

The `fr_trace` analysis aggregates per-rank pickles and shows states and sequence numbers. A collective with matching `collective_seq_id` across ranks but a missing rank points at the rank that never arrived.

`TORCH_FR_BUFFER_SIZE` and `TORCH_NCCL_DUMP_ON_TIMEOUT` are PyTorch recorder controls. `NCCL_DEBUG` and `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS` are NCCL transport controls. Before PyTorch 2.9 the buffer variables carried `TORCH_NCCL_` names that still work with a warning.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, list the three variables that arm dump-on-timeout and the analysis command: `TORCH_FR_BUFFER_SIZE=2000`, `TORCH_NCCL_DUMP_ON_TIMEOUT=1`, `TORCH_FR_DUMP_TEMP_FILE=/tmp/fr`, then `python -m torch.distributed.flight_recorder.fr_trace` on the dump directory.
traps: Mixing recorder and transport layers. `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` shows devices and sockets, not which Python collective mismatched.
Using the pre-2.9 buffer names without knowing they warn. Old and new names both arm the recorder, but only the new names are quiet.
Expecting NCCL flight dumps from CPU-only ranks. Collection is NCCL-gated, so on CPU read provided dumps instead of claiming local collection.

selfTest.q: What does the desync report add over a bare timeout?
selfTest.a: It names which collective and which rank fell out of step, instead of leaving every rank parked in the same wait with no attribution.

selfTest.q: The aggregated dump shows a collective with `missing_ranks` holding one rank. What does that mean?
selfTest.a: That rank never reached the collective with the matching sequence number. It is the first suspect; the waiting ranks are victims.

selfTest.q: Which controls belong to PyTorch and which to NCCL?
selfTest.a: PyTorch owns the recorder buffer, dump-on-timeout and dump path. NCCL owns `NCCL_DEBUG`, `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS`, interface selection and transport logging.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: diagnose one injected hang from per-rank dumps, naming the first-cause rank and the victim ranks.
units.stopWhen: You can arm the recorder variables from memory and read a desync plus fr_trace output down to the first-cause rank.

fit.note: Both Flight Recorder generations plus the Stas desync and transport sections cover concepts and dump reading; hang diagnosis practice sits in the mini-project.

study.title: Overlap math and roofline tables
study.locator: Communication-Computation Overlap with the overlap inequality and the 7B worked step, and The Memory Wall and Roofline Diagnosis with the intensity table

study.title: Overlap in practice
study.locator: Chapter 4, Overlapping Communication and Computation (Pipelining), with Achieving Maximal Overlap in Practice and Distributed Data Parallel Strategies

focus: Intensity is \(I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{bytes}\). Above the ridge (near 295 FLOP per byte for H100 FP16) the op is compute bound; below it, memory bound. Communication bound means exposed collective time dominates the step.
Exposed communication is total collective time minus the overlapped part. Overlap needs asynchronous buckets or prefetch on separate streams plus enough compute to hide the transfer.
Small messages are launch bound, not bandwidth bound. Doubling bytes halves the bandwidth term but leaves the latency term, so the factor-of-two slogans fail there.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute intensity for the JAX Q1 case (about 17M bytes, about 1.07G FLOPs, \(I \approx 63\)) and label it memory bound against a ridge of 295. Then state the exposed-communication formula as total minus overlapped time.
traps: Claiming overlap from asynchronous issue alone. Concurrency needs timeline proof that compute and communication actually coincide.
Quoting reduce-scatter as twice as fast as all-reduce without regime. The factor holds for equal payload in the bandwidth-bound limit only.
Treating intensity as a hardware constant. It is a property of the op shape and batch; the ridge is the hardware property.

selfTest.q: Intensity 63 against ridge 295: which bound?
selfTest.a: Memory bound. Achievable throughput is bandwidth times intensity, well below peak FLOPs.

selfTest.q: What is exposed communication?
selfTest.a: Collective time not hidden under compute: total communication minus the overlapped portion, measured from aligned timelines.

selfTest.q: How do you prove overlap instead of mere asynchrony?
selfTest.a: Show concurrent compute and communication intervals on aligned rank timelines with dependencies that permit concurrency, not just nonblocking calls.

selfTest.q: When does the reduce-scatter factor-of-two claim break?
selfTest.a: For small latency-bound messages and across different algorithms or fabrics. It moves about half the bytes of an equal-payload all-reduce only in the bandwidth-bound limit.

study.locator: DataLoader section with `num_workers`, pinned memory and `non_blocking` device copy, plus the num-workers-bench.py and pin-memory-non-block-bench.py results

study.title: Storage benchmarking for training
study.locator: Benchmarks section with `fio` for throughput, IOPS and latency, and DLIO for the training-like I/O pattern without accelerators

focus: With `num_workers=0` the accelerator blocks on fetch and transforms. Sweep workers and watch iteration time plus CPU saturation; two workers often suffice and more can hang dual loaders.
`pin_memory=True` with `non_blocking=True` plus prefetch hides host-to-device transfer. Measure with and without; pinned memory alone without async copy buys little.
Sequential versus random reads, local NVMe versus shared filesystem, and preprocessing on CPU versus GPU are different limits. `fio` tests the device; DLIO tests the training pattern.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, sweep `num_workers` from 0 to 4 on a synthetic transform-bound loader, plot mean iteration time with `pin_memory` on and off, and name the worker count where the curve flattens with CPU saturation as evidence.
traps: Adding workers until the problem disappears. Dual-loader hangs and diminishing returns need a measured optimum, not a maximum.
Setting `pin_memory=True` without `non_blocking=True`. Pinned staging without asynchronous copy still blocks the transfer.
Blaming the interconnect for storage starvation. A slow filesystem or random-read pattern starves every rank identically.

selfTest.q: Iteration time falls from 5.4 s to 0.8 s as workers go 0 to 3, then stalls. What do you conclude?
selfTest.a: Input was the bound up to 3 workers, then compute or another stage dominates. Adding a fourth worker buys nothing; confirm with CPU saturation and trace attribution.

selfTest.q: Why pair `pin_memory` with `non_blocking`?
selfTest.a: Pinned memory enables DMA while nonblocking copy lets the transfer overlap compute. Either alone leaves most of the transfer exposed.

selfTest.q: When does `fio` mislead about training input?
selfTest.a: When the pattern differs: `fio` reports device throughput and IOPS, while training does small random reads with preprocessing. DLIO emulates the loader pattern.

Separate memory fixes from numerical effects of precision or offload changes.

study.locator: Chapter 13, Profiling and Tuning Memory in PyTorch, with Tuning the CUDA Memory Allocator, Activation Checkpointing for Memory Savings, and Offloading Parameters to CPU and NVMe

study.title: Graph breaks and recompilations
study.locator: Chapter 14, Explaining and Minimizing Graph Breaks, with Graph Breaks and TorchDynamo explain(), Minimize Graph Recompilations, and Debugging Compiler Phases, Graph Breaks, and Performance

study.title: OOM triage and fragmentation fixes
study.locator: Debugging CUDA OOM in forward and backward, Overcoming CUDA OOM due to memory fragmentation with expandable segments, and the memory profiler plus allocation tracing sections

focus: Free memory with no large-enough block is fragmentation; a spike at a known layer is an activation peak; growth across steps is a leak. `torch.cuda.memory_stats` plus the snapshot timeline separates the three.

Fix in order: reserve exact behavior first, then allocator settings, then activation checkpointing or offload. Each change keeps an equivalence check so memory savings do not silently change numerics.
`torch._dynamo.explain` plus `TORCH_LOGS` with graph breaks and recompiles names the break. Dynamic shapes and data-dependent branches add guards; each new guard shape recompiles.
units.reproduce: Without notes, enable the memory snapshot around one training step, capture the peak segment, and explain from the timeline whether the peak is parameters, activations or temporaries. Then run `torch._dynamo.explain` on a toy function with a data-dependent branch and name the break.
traps: Shrinking the batch for a fragmentation OOM. Smaller tensors can fragment worse; expandable segments or staged allocation often fixes the real cause.
Enabling checkpointing without accounting for the extra forward FLOPs. HFU rises while MFU stays flat, and step time changes for a known reason.
Allowing `allow_in_graph` as a quick fix for every break. It bypasses safety checks and can silently produce wrong results.

selfTest.q: Memory shows 10 GB free but a 2 GB allocation fails. What is the likely cause?
selfTest.a: Fragmentation: no single free block fits 2 GB. Check the block-size histogram and expandable-segments behavior before changing the model.

selfTest.q: Peak memory lands on activations at long sequence. Which fixes preserve the update?
selfTest.a: Activation checkpointing with recomputation, or offload with correct restore. Both keep the mathematical update while trading compute or transfer for memory.

selfTest.q: Step time jumps after adding a print of a tensor value. What happened?
